HMW-V12: Bag Package List on Vendor Job Detail

Design hypothesis — Teleport OS Vendor · 2026-08-10

"How might we show a trip's bag package list on the vendor job detail page so dispatchers and drivers can verify cargo at pickup against the system of record?"
Context: When an FM driver arrives at the pickup warehouse, they need to verify that the bags they're loading match what Teleport's system expects — correct bag numbers, count, weights, origins. Currently vendors reconcile this from WhatsApp messages or their own spreadsheets. VUS-013 calls for showing the bag list on the job detail page. The data model already has BagPackage (bagNumber, weightKg, origin, destination, pickupDate, mawb, assignedTripId). A single trip typically has 6–80 bags; large cross-border shipments can reach 200+.

Option A — Inline scrollable bag table (below Cargo)

A dedicated "Bag Packages" section inserted between Cargo and Proof of Service. Renders as a compact table with a fixed max-height and overflow scroll. The section header shows the bag count so users can see total at a glance without expanding. The driver physically cross-references bag numbers on screen against physical stickers as they load.

Pros
• Zero extra interaction — bag list is always visible when relevant
• Fixed scroll area keeps page length predictable regardless of bag count
• Works as a verification instrument: driver scans physical bags top-to-bottom, matching against the screen
• Weight total in footer lets driver confirm aggregate without mental math
• No new UI pattern — same table/section pattern used throughout the app
Cons
• Adds ~200px of height to the page even for small lists (6 bags)
• No search or filter — finding a specific bag in a 200+ list requires scrolling
• Scrollable table within a scrollable page is awkward on touch screens
• Section will show as empty for non-FM or early-stage jobs with no bag data yet

Option B — Collapsible accordion, collapsed by default

A collapsible section header showing aggregate: "Bag Packages · 24 bags · 1,247 kg". Collapsed by default. Expanding reveals the same table as Option A. Dispatchers who trust the count don't need to open it. Drivers at pickup expand it when physically loading bags.

Pros
• Page stays compact for users who only need the aggregate count
• Summary header (24 bags · 1,247 kg) is enough for most reconciliation use cases
• Proof section never pushed far below the fold
• Can expand before physical pickup and collapse after confirming
Cons
• Hides the most critical verification data behind an extra click
• Collapsed by default trains users not to look at it — "accordion blindness"
• Aggregate in summary duplicates what the Cargo section already shows
• Inconsistent with design system — no other sections on this page use an accordion pattern

Option C — Summary row + searchable bottom sheet

The Cargo section shows "24 bags · 1,247 kg" as today plus a "[View List →]" link. Tapping opens a bottom sheet/drawer with a searchable bag table — allowing dispatch to find "SHWK000012" instantly in a 200-bag list. The sheet covers roughly 75% of the viewport and has a sticky header with a bag number search input.

Pros
• Search field solves the 200-bag problem — driver types partial bag number to jump directly
• Page layout is clean and short — nothing pushes Proof section down
• Bottom sheet pattern is familiar from mobile apps; works well on 768px tablets
• Pickup date column fits naturally in the sheet without cluttering the detail page
Cons
• Introduces a modal pattern not used anywhere else in the vendor app (design inconsistency)
• Closes if the user accidentally taps outside — frustrating mid-loading
• "View bag list →" link is subtle — not obvious enough for high-urgency pickup verification
• Admin slide-out panel is the only overlay pattern in the platform; a bottom sheet is a second overlay type

Decision: Option A — Inline scrollable table

Recommendation: Implement the bag package list as an always-visible, inline scrollable table in a dedicated "Bag Packages" section between Cargo and Proof of Service. Use max-height: 200px; overflow-y: auto to contain long lists without introducing a separate interaction layer.

Rationale: The bag list is a verification instrument — it has to be visible the moment a dispatcher opens the job detail to brief a driver or when a driver physically loads bags. Hiding it behind an accordion (Option B) trains users to ignore it. A bottom sheet (Option C) introduces an unrelated overlay pattern to an app that uses full-page detail, not modals. "Every pixel shows data" — if the data exists and is operationally relevant, show it.

Placement: Between Cargo (aggregate) and Proof of Service. Placing it right after Cargo creates a logical narrative: aggregate summary → detailed breakdown → evidence of completion. For non-FM jobs or trips with no bag data, the section is omitted entirely (no empty-state noise).

Columns: Bag # · Weight · Origin · Destination. Pickup date is omitted from the inline table (all bags in the trip share the same pickup date, shown in the Route section). MAWB is in the page header. Destination is typically the same for all bags on a trip but included so drivers can verify cross-destination splits if they exist.

Open question: For the WeChat Mini Program (TODO-049/HMW-V09), should the driver see the same bag list on their screen for scan-as-you-load verification? If yes, the data model already supports it — the WeChat screen can mirror this section. This would close the verification loop: Teleport system → dispatcher sees list → driver scans at pickup → discrepancy surfaces in-app instead of at customs.
